speechtext:
With respect to the licensing of steam trawlers, Mr. Speaker, it may be of interest to recall the conditions under which steam trawling was begun in this country. Some years ago those who were engaged in the marketing of fish found that steadiness of supply was essential in order to increase the demand, and at that time there was no assurance of such steadiness of supply, particularly in the winter season. Hence in 1910 steam trawling was initiated with one vessel. With the development of the demand for fresh fish the number was increased to two in 1912 and in the following year to five.
During the war the demand grew rapidly, and probably the number of trawlers would have been increased more rapidly than it was had they been available. The largest number operated in the war period was eight in 1918. In 1926 the number had increased to eleven, and since then it has declined.
Following consideration of the majority and minority reports of the Atlantic Fisheries Commission of 1927-28, legislation for the better control of trawlers was adopted in 1929. The main provisions of this legislation were:
(a)	All trawlers must be licensed.
(b)	All trawlers should be registered in Canada and owned by Canadian companies or persons.
(c)	That trawler fishing should not be allowed within twelve miles of the shore.
(d)	That the minister may determine the number of trawlers to be licensed.
(e)	That regulations might be made by order in council prescribing the evidence to be submitted with applications for licences fixing the conditions under which licences should be issued and making any other provisions respecting licences.
By order in council of October 30, 1929, regulations were adopted under the authority of the new legislation. These regulations provided for the licensing of trawlers and for a fee of one cent per pound on all cod, haddock and halibut that were landed by foreign built trawlers and two-thirds of a cent a pound on all such fish that were landed by Canadian built trawlers, excepting on fish landed during the months of January, February and March each year, when no fee would be charged.
One of the trawler operating companies failed to pay the licence fee, and action was taken in the exchequer court to compel payment. This resulted in a decision of that court of the 9th of March, 1931, that the regulations w'ere ultra vires. After further consideration of the matter new regulations were adopted by order in council of August 14, 1931. These provided for a lioence fee of S500 for each trawler and that the applicant must furnish the minister with evidence that would satisfy him that the applicant could not obtain an adequate supply of suitable fish to enable him- properly to conduct and develop his business from the hook and line fishermen, and that the granting of the licence would not adversely affect the extent to which fish would be purchased from the hook and line fishermen.
Following the submission of applications, which were accompanied by the necessary evidence supported by declarations, licences for six trawlers were granted for the fiscal year 1932-33. Five of these were for trawlers operated by the Maritime-National company and one by the Leonard fisheries.
Fishermen's organizations and boards of trade have strongly urged that no trawlers be
Trawler Licences

licensed for the present fiscal year. On the other hand, the Halifax board of trade and the mayor of Halifax have urged very strongly the renewal of all the existing licences. Applications for renewal of the five licences held by the Maritime-National company have been made, and the Leonard Fisheries has intimated that it intends to apply for a renewal of its licence.
At this point it may be interesting to note that the decline in the trawler catch in recent years has kept pace with the decline in the hook and line catch. In Nova Scotia alone the hook and line catch of the kinds of fish landed by trawlers was 150,200,977 pounds. The trawler catch that year was 31,365,423 pounds. Last year the Nova Scotia catch of these fish by the hook and line fishermen was 108,645,871 pounds, while the catch by the steam trawlers was 22,956,729 pounds, or a decrease of practically 27 per cent in each case.
It is also contended that the trawler operators are amongst the largest purchasers of fish from the hook and line fishermen, and the former maintain -that it is only possible for them to continue to make such large purchases from the hook and line fishermen because of having the trawlers so that they can keep continuously in the market. It is also contended that the main landings by the trawlers are during the six winter months when hook and line fishing is reduced to a minimum, and during a portion of which no licence fee was charged on the trawler landings under the previous regulations.
It also may be of value to note that all dtther countries are allowing trawlers to operate. Out of European ports about 5,000 of these vessels are operating yearly. Out of United States ports there are usually over 300. These latter vessels as well as a large number from France and sometimes from other European countries, fish on the Banks adjacent to our coasts, so that even if our trawlers were withdrawn it would decrease the amount of trawling on these Banks by a very small proportion only.
After consideration of all the facts it is thought that if the Maritime-National had three trawlers instead of five operating they could reasonably assure the steadiness of supply as well as the proportion of haddock needed. Hence it has been decided that for the present year that company will be allowed three trawlers and the Leonard Fisheries one, as before. There are no other applicants. This will involve a reduction in number of 33 J per cent. This reduction will be put
[Mr. Duranleau.J
into effect from the first of May, thus giving one month to the company to enable it to fill certain contracts into which it has entered.

There is one other matter which has been called to my attention since last evening. There is an anomaly in the Penitentiary Act as it now stands by reason of an amendment to the criminal code passed in 1929. Under that amendment the crown was permitted to appeal in criminal cases; in other words, where a man was tried for a crime and the charge against him was dismissed, the crown was permitted to enter an appeal. In many cases the prisoner was forced to remain in gaol pending the hearing of the appeal because he was unable to furnish bail. Sometimes a man would spend three, four or five months waiting the result of the appeal. Under 'the provisions of the Penitentiary Act as it now stands on the statute books, the time spent in gaol pending trial shall not be credited on the length of the sentence and it is now proposed to amend that section by providing the following:
Any period during which a convict is detained in the gaol or other place of confinement pursuant to the authority of this section shall not be computed as time served in the execution of his sentence unless he be so detained pending an appeal by the attorney general or counsel for the crown.
If the crown appeals and the charge against the man is subsequently abandoned or dismissed, the time spent in gaol pending appeal shall be considered as part of the sentence.

I wish now to say a few words concerning the unemploment situation as it applies to the textile industry. The other industries I have to do with are certainly in a very serious condition. Anything which has to do with furniture, or any of the iron working industries, is in bad shape. Personally I do not think 5371&-233J

The one bright spot in my particular part of the country is the textile industry, and perhaps hon. members will pardon me if for a few moments I speak concerning it. For several years in this house I have argued that certain lines of the textile industry-and in
The Budget-Mr. Edwards

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that Canadian wool?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will come to Canadian wool in a moment. One of the most encouraging features to-day in the woollen branch of the textile business is the increased use of Canadian wool. I have taken the trouble to make inquiries regarding this feature. Prior to the revision of the tariff on worsted yarns in 1930, the combing and spinning plants of the country were practically closed, the reason being that worsted yarns were duty free. As a result yarn could be imported from England for less than the cost of production in Canada. This was due to the different wage schedules and other charges imposed on Canadian mills such as workmen's compensation, minimum wage laws and so on, which did not obtain in England. From the time the ten per cent duty was taken off in 1927, therefore, the combing and spinning plants of this country were practically closed, and no Canadian wool could be used. It was shipped out of the country. It is worthy of note that the arguments used by the Canadian mills when they protested against the removal of the ten per cent duty was used in turn by the English mills to protect themselves against yarns imported into England from mid-European countries.
I should like to illustrate this position. Dominion Woollens and Worsteds, Limited, have a large plant in my constituency at Hespeler, Ontario, with subsidiary spinning plants at Milton and Orillia. Prior to 1930, the Orillia
The Budget-Mr. Edwards

and Milton plants were closed, and the Hespeler mill had about 600 employees working part time. Since that time the Orillia plant has been re-opened and is running today with 60 to 80 employees on full time. The Milton plant ran for a short time but the equipment from this mill was moved to Hespeler for reasons of economy but the equipment is still in operation. The payroll of the Hespeler and Orillia mills has averaged from 800 to 830 employees this winter, with from 60 to 80 of these employees at Orillia.
One of the most encouraging features today is the increased use of Canadian wool in the products of these mills. Three years ago practically no Canadian wool of any kind was used in the Hespeler mill. To-day, however, the combing department is operated as a commission combing department for the wool trade, and is consuming Canadian wool at the rate of 3,000,000 pounds a year in the greasy or unscoured state. The tops produced are being distributed bjr wool dealers throughout the entire worsted spinning industry. This development appears to be in its infancy and, I believe, the use of Canadian wool will expand very quickly to a much larger figure.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

What percentage of the

I could not say exactly. The combing department employs from 50 to 60 people, and it is estimated that the dealers handling the wool employ another 50 people. Three years ago the percentage of Canadian wool used in the manufacture of worsteds in Canada was practically nil; to-day all the medium and coarse quality cloth produced contains about 50 per cent of Canadian wool and this proportion is increasing steadily. It is estimated that within the next six or eight months at least two-thirds of the material in medium and coarse cloths will be Canadian wool. This wool is not being used in this plant in the manufacture of the finer qualities of cloth, but other manufacturers who are buying tops combed there appear to be using large quantities of botany wool grown in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
The question of dealing with wool prices is an extremely difficult one. The trouble is that the farmer sells on a grease basis at so much per pound, the wool including the natural

grease and acquired dirt, while the manufacturer buys on a clean content basis even though he may pay so much per pound in the grease. For example, a manufacturer has offered to him two wools which, when clean, can be used for the same purpose. I just want to deal with these two samples of wool in order to explain the variations in prices. For the first sample the manufacturer pays 8 cents per pound in the grease; there is a freight charge of 2 cents per pound and a scouring charge of 2 cents per pound, with a 50 per cent shrink. For the second sample the manufacturer pays 12 cents per pound in the grease; there is a freight charge of 2 cents per pound and a scouring charge of 2 cents per pound, with a shrink of 25 per cent. The clean cost to the manufacturer for one pound of wool would be: for the first sample, 16 cents for the wool, 4 cents for freight and 4 cents for scouring, or a total of 24 cents. For the second sample the cost would be 15 cents for the wool, 2J cents for freight and 2} cents for scouring, or a total of 20 cents. In addition there is a large number of different types of wool to deal with.
I hope I have made the situation clear with regard to the woollen and worsted part of the textile industry. I do not profess to know anything at all about the cotton end of the business, but the figures I have given in connection with woollens, including worsteds and worsted yarns, are absolutely correct.
I should like to conclude, Mr. Speaker, with a word of appreciation for the splendid manner in which this government, has handled the situation. We are in extremely difficult times, to get out of which it will be necessary for hon. members on all sides to cooperate. There is no panic in this country. The people are satisfied with the present government; and headed by the right hon. gentleman who leads it, will emerge from this situation. If the Prime Minister is given proper assistance he will pull us ou't of our present difficulty, and I am sure that we shall recover long before other countries that lack our natural resources are able to return to normal. The indomitable spirit of the Canadian people will triumph.

speechtext:
The discussion of the budget is always the most important debate that takes place in the House of Commons in any session. I am afraid I Shall not have time to deal with the arguments put forward by those who have preceded me in the present discussion, but so far as the presentation of the budget itself is concerned, I desire, in

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
common with others, to congratulate the minister. He made a splendid presentation of a very difficult subject. I do not think that in the history of Canada any Minister of Finance has had to face as difficult a problem as the present minister in presenting his budget to this house. For three successive years this country, with the rest of the world, has been suffering from a very severe depression. Let us try to be as fair as we possibly can. With other countries we have been suffering in consequence of that depression. Now the minister takes a great deal of credit from the fact that Canada, according to his statement, is not quite so badly off as other countries; he suggests that we have not suffered quite so much. I can hardly agree with that statement; I believe that the position which we occupy to-day, if matters were properly managed by the government, would not be as bad as it is, and many of the difficulties through which we are passing at the present time could be avoided.
I will not take time to recount the various promises which the present Prime Minister gave to the country when he was appealing for its support. Those promises have been frequently referred to in this house, and with one single exception the right hon. gentleman has failed to implement them. He has not carried out the promises which he made with so much vigour and force during the election. Indeed, many hon. gentlemen opposite owe their seats in this house to those promises made by their leader. I am not going to discuss the promises he gave the people, but there is one promise which I am bound to say he has kept, a promise that has had the most serious consequences for the people of Canada, and that is the promise to increase the tariffs of the country to the point where he would give protection to every industry in Canada and shut out imports. He has kept that promise one hundred per cent. I am glad that hon. gentlemen opposite applaud that statement; I am glad that farmers particularly applaud it, because if there is any comfort to a farmer in the faot that our tariffs have been increased to the extent they have been, I should like to see him rise in his place and say so.
I have listened with a good deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Edwards). He comes from a manufacturing centre and finds that on the average the tariff of seventy per cent on textiles has been of immense benefit to the industry in his locality. He frankly admits however that the furniture industry has
severely suffered in consequence. Let us give credit to the government for having kept this one promise. Let us give them all the credit that is coming to them for the fact that the world is passing through a period of depression. At the same time let us look into the faats for a few moments to see whether or not hon. gentlemen opposite have helped to improve the situation in Canada.
What was the great difficulty in 1930, according to Conservative speakers at that time? My hon. friends were not complaining about the financial situation in Canada. I venture to say that ninety-five per cent of them had no complaint to make about any suffering among the manufacturers. The manufacturers were fairly prosperous in this country. I suppose my hon. friend who has just taken his seat will take issue with me on that point so far as the textile industry is concerned. With the single exception of that particular industry, and the woollen part of that industry, there was certainly no serious complaint from the manufacturers, for they had enjoyed a period of prosperity never before known in any previous period in the history of Canada. They all admitted that. Unemployment was the evil that had to be cured. We had 117,000 unemployed in Canada-and I am quoting the words of the Prime Minister, which no doubt were repeated by other hon. gentlemen on the opposite side. There were 117,000 unemployed, and we rushed through increases in the tariff in the short session of 1930-to do what? In order to protect industry in Canada but primarily, as we were told, to cure unemployment. In connection with unemployment we were assured that another thing which was to be deplored would be remedied; there was to be no system of doles in Canada, but everyone was to be furnished with work.
Now, what is the record? I have no time to go into details, but hon. gentlemen opposite frankly admit that there are to-day in Canada nearly 900,000 people out of work. The question is:	Have tariffs helped to relieve
unemployment or on the contrary have they contributed' to the present situation? Undoubtedly they have, and that is the answer to the application of high tariffs as a means of aiding unemployment. What else has it done? We had fairly prosperous farmers in this country in 1930. There was not very much complaint in 1930 in regard to the returns from farming operations. Well, what is the condition of the farmers to-day, not only in the west but in Ontario, which as is so frequently stated in this house is the banner province of the dominion? That is the estimate for this year and it may not amount to that much. It is casting the treasury of Canada more than $140,000,000 to continue exorbitant tariff protection of this kind. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) did very well the other day with a bad subject. He succeeded in making himself believe, if he did not make anyone else believe, that Canada was not in such a bad condition. He stated it was unfair to use dollars and cents in making comparisons, that we should use volume in order to explain the real position of Canada. Unfortunately volume does not take our wheat out of the country, nor does it take care of our cattle. The government states it is going to do something, but this is the greatest to-morrow government I have ever seen. It has been going to do things for the past three or four years.
When the Minister of Finance delivered his budget I had hoped that his speech would show that he and his government realized that the imposition of these high duties was the cause to a large degree of the difficulty through which we are now passing. I had hoped there would be some remission in the-tariff, but there was not a sign except as it affected certain manufacturers and their raw products. I am not alone in this opinion, the best economists in the world hold with this position. Hon. gentlemen will say that other countries have done certain things and Canada would suffer if she did not follow suit. In reply to that I would refer them to the last

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
four years of the Liberal administration. Other countries were putting up their duties to an unprecedented degree and vve did not seem to suffer very much as a consequence because we were able to make agreements with other countries. I had hoped that our tariff had been raised to such a point that it could be used in making favourable trade treaties with other countries willing to trade with us. Did it work out in that way? I need only refer to what the Prime Minister said when he attended the trade conference in England in 1930. He was not willing to trade with Great Britain and give her a chance to get her goods into this country. Hon. gentlemen may talk until they are tired about the encouragement given to empire trade by the conference agreements, but so long as Canada maintains her present position and refuses to buy, we poor individuals engaged in the primary industries will be unable to sell our products. It is futile to talk about blasting, that does not mean anything.
What has the government been forced to resort to? It has been forced to the subsidizing of the natural products of the country. There is also talk of reducing the wheat acreage and other matters of this kind. It is said we have overproduction but hon. members who have given any thought to this matter know perfectly well that we have not overproduction-our trouble is under-consumption. Do hon. members mean to tell me that the 1,300,000 people being fed by the government are consuming all they are capable of consuming? Not at all. The same thing applies to the people in other countries where similar policies are being pursued. Because other countries are carrying on a policy of trade restriction, it is said that Canada should follow suit. Such a policy is costing the treasury of this country more money than we can possibly estimate. I do not mean to say that under a different policy we would be able to collect $244,000,000; not at all, but I do say that we would not have the tremendous drop in revenue which has occurred through the infliction of these excessive duties with the consequent restrictions of trade.
In the forty minutes at my disposal I am not able to go very far into this matter, but I should like to deal with another point raised the other night by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He referred to the stabilization of the wheat market through the injection of assistance by the federal government. I have sold and raised wheat for the past twenty-five or thirty years and may I say to the minister that whatever advantage this step may have been in 1930 and 1931, it certainly was no
advantage in 1932. Do hon. members mean to tell me that the government stabilized that market when, after they went into it, wheat which was selling at sixty cento a bushel, began to go down? Were we foolish enough to believe the government weTe stabilizing that market when the price of wheat would drop four or five cento a bushel within a day, until it reached the low price of forty cents, the lowest it has ever been since I have been engaged in farming in western Canada. I am bound to think and still believe if the market had been left alone, we farmers who produce the grain would have had more from our products than we have under the circumstances that exist. I have not time to go into details in that connection, but examining these orders in council and looking into the whole matter of what they fondly call stabilization of the Canadian market and what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said the other night, namely, that Canada played a very important part in stabilizing prices throughout the world, let me say to him that it is not such an important part Canadian products play in the stabilization of world prices.

speechtext:
The hon.
member may say it if he likes. One does not believe that sort of thing. So far as the stabilization of the Canadian market is concerned, if my hon. friend takes any comfort out of that, then I shall say to him that I would like a better explanation than the one he was able to give the other evening when presenting the case to the house.
Another matter the government seemed to be determined to preserve was the sanctity of the dollar; we must remain on the gold standard. It will be remembered that a few weeks ago we had in this house a vote on which most of us on this side voted for the placing of the dollar on a parity with sterling. I recognize some difficulty in this connection, but we were told by the Prime Minister that the government stood for a sound dollar and that there would be no inflation which it was assumed there would be were we to attempt
3692	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Steioart (Edmonton)
to place our currency on a parity with sterling. It was plain that to do so would reduce the value of the Canadian dollar to a very low point. To-day I made inquiry and I find that exchange is twenty cents; that the Canadian dollar is worth eighty cents in New York. That is what we have to pay if we wish to exchange Canadian currency into United States funds.	_	_
We were warned also that, this being the case, the situation in Canada would become serious. Let us examine this for a moment or two. According to the statement issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day, we owe in the neighbourhood of $3,700,000,000. It is assumed that the provinces and municipalities owe something in the neighbourhood of over $2,000,000,000, making a total of about $6,000,000,000, and that corporations and individuals owe in the neighbourhood of $2,500,000,000, bringing the total to about $9,000,000,000. If we take the whole amount, fully one-half of it is owed in Canada; the other half is owed in the United States and abroad. The first benefit from inflation would be that it would help the situation in Canada in connection with at least one-half of our obligations and to some extent, not altogether, offset the increase in our obligations abroad. In the second place we would not be talking to-day about stabilization of the items mentioned in the budget if we were on somewhat of a parity with sterling and we would not be having the complaints from hon. members on this side and from hon. members opposite, if they would speak their minds, regarding the selection of a restricted number of commodities. This benefit would apply to every Canadian commodity marketed in the old country; we would get the benefit all along the line. Hon. gentlemen say that they are going to increase prices by something like fifty or sixty cents on the British pound on all the goods on the selected list sold in Great Britain. If that is the case, the goods that are not mentioned will have to take a reduction of fifty or sixty cents on the pound sterling. The argument must be good both ways. Therefore the advantage to be obtained by inflation far ouit-weighs the bugaboo held out that our exchange will cost us too much and it will be the ruination of the credit of Canada. Let us see what happened in Australia-I have a quotation which puts the matter much more tersely and better than I could:
Two years ago the people of Australia confronted a situation more desperate and more disheartening than the people of Canada have ever faced. But to-day Australia is the most prosperous part of the British Empire.

We were told that Canada was, but apparently this economist does not think so.
The six and a half million people of that dominion found themselves two years ago saddled with the colossal debt of $5,000,000,000, their solvency despaired of, their export restricted, unemployment growing, and all the influences of the world-wide depression breaking upon (them as they did upon the people of Canada.
Australia has not defaulted one dollar of its interest payments abroad, and has not asked outside creditors to cut down their claims. These obligations hiave been met in full. The spread of unemployment has been checked, and the movement turned in the other direction. Business is on the upgrade. Exports have expanded. Deflation has not been allowed to run riot there. The farmers are drawing twice as much per bushel for their wheat as the farmers of western Canada. The country is buoyant with hope, money is cheap and plentiful and public credit has been restored.
I very well remember it was stated in the house the credit of Australia was doubtful two years ago.
These changes did not come about by chance. They were the direct and calculated results of public policy. Instead of submitting to the depression, Australia has fought it, and won. The government of Canada has let depression dictate conditions, with the results that we see, and another tax-raising budget as the latest of them. The government of Australia has actually started to reduce taxation!
There were three steps in the program by which Australia countered the change in world conditions. The first was a revaluation of the currency. The gold standard W'as abandoned and the Australian pound hitched to the British pound. Export trade went up to 26 per cent more than in the previous peak year. Australia had no wheat carry-over last summer. Her farmers sold out their crop at from 60 to 75 cents a bushel at point of delivery. Our farmers sold at half the price, and 130,000.000 bushels had not left the country when the shipping year ended.
As a second step, Australia increased the amount of its currency, otherwise "inflated," but only to a limited extent. That should interest our stand-pat economists who say inflation cannot be controlled. Australia has controlled it. It has applied no farther than to modify the ruinous process of deflation, that has been allowed to have full swing in Canada.
The third step was a plan of national economy. But the "economy" was not made to fall only on the civil servants, wage earners and poorer classes. Australian holders of public securities were asked to accept a cut of 221 per cent in interest rates. To their eternal credit, 97 per cent of them did so voluntarily, and only three per cent from compulsion. Interest on mortgages was cut 22J per cent.
A conversion loan was offered to the public. The result is particularly significant. Whereas the old six per cent bonds had fallen to 80, the new four per cent conversion bonds went up to 102. The bond holders who had sacrificed 22J per cent of their interest found themselves with their whole capital in hand. That shows what the Australians think of the way the

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
depression has been met and what they think about the future. It shows also that they have money to invest.

speechtext:
Why can we not do something of this kind in Canada? I have heard some reasons given, but frankly I cannot agree with them. Why is it that we drift on from year to year with no concrete plan for improvement? Why is it that we are simply waiting for the economic conference, the date of which has not yet been fixed? And all the time the load of debt taxation is increased from year to year, and we come to the end of the year in what condition? This year my hon. friend has to borrow $156,000,000 to supply what he should have received from the taxpayers of this country, and he has had to do the same thing every year since this government took office. How long can we keep going un.der those conditions? There has been added to the public debt of this country nearly $500,000,000, since the government took office. To-morrow I suppose we shall be discussing the railway bill because the railways are suffering for lack of business. To my mind, 75 per cent of the cause of that lack of business are the trade restrictions that have been imposed which kill traffic. What does my hon. friend propose to do about the railways? The government are appointing trustees, trustees in bankruptcy practically, to take care of the national railways of this country. I picked up the paper the other day and read that the drop in earnings of the Canadian National Railways for February over February of last year was $800,000, and that the drop in earnings of the Canadian Pacific was $132,000 over February of last year. Is it not time that drastic remedies be thought of in connection with public affairs in this country? Is it not time that we began to realize that the abyss spoken of by the Prime Minister is much nearer than many of us thought?
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we have to do something. What other indications do I see that the government are feeling a bit serious about the situation of this country after three years
of their policies? Just a day or so ago they took the right by order in council to depart from the gold standard. I say to them in all sincerity that if they had taken that step long ago we would have had some benefit, but as it stands we seem to have all the evils and none of the advantages of staying on the gold standard. I say to them now that one of the first things they should do is to pass that order in council right away. Let them abandon this idea of bonusing the natural products of this country exported to the United Kingdom, and instead let them spread the advantage over the whole gamut of exports to Great Britain and let every producer get the advantage. I am entirely in favour of that kind of policy. I feel that perhaps the government will do it, and I pray to the Lord that they will do it. I hope that one of the first orders in council they will pass will be that very order.
Have we not arrived at the place, Mr. Speaker, where we cannot afford to borrow any more money. I believe every thoughtful man in this country realizes that. Indeed, how are we going to borrow any more money when we cannot to-day pay the interest on what we have already borrowed? We are now borrowing money to pay the interest upon borrowed capital. That is the situation of this country to-day. How long would an individual last who found himself in that position financially? Yet no one will deny that that is the position in which we find ourselves. We need not talk about the western provincial governments and their difficulties, because a part of their difficulties is a result of these obnoxious tariffs which I have mentioned; that and the excessive taxation in this country. I do not say that that is the whole cause of their difficulties. I do not defend them. I know that they have been reckless in expenditure for many years, but something has got to be done, and done quickly. I doubt very much if Canada can continue to feed 1,300,000 people very much longer. Then what are we going to do about it?
I noticed that the other day a delegation came to see the Prime Minister and urged the government to engage in a building program on borrowed money. I was relieved the other day when the Prime Minister stated in this house, in reply to an inquiry as to what effect inflation might have, that many years ago this country did inflate to the extent of S68,-000,000, and no particular harm was done. We could not discover any evil consequences. The exchange did not go very seriously against us, and up to this day we 'have not yet discovered that that inflation worked any detri-
3694	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
ment to Canada's position. Since that time the Canadian dollar has at times been at a premium in the United States. I have no fear, speaking for myself, of inflation at the present moment. I support it and believe in it. Not only that, but I would suggest to the government that in every city in Canada there are public buildings required in the public service of this country which might be constructed. This work could be begun at once. The government could take the responsibility of issuing currency for the purpose of constructing needed public buildings in every city in this country. Let them take this responsibility as it was taken in 1915, as depicted by the Prime Minister. If they are afraid of the effects so far as exchange is concerned, let them put a clause in the agreement reducing the issue by annual instalments from revenue for a period of fifteen years. The note issue will be reduced and we shall have the improvements and we shall have added nothing to the public debt on that account. The interest charges that we would have to pay on borrowed money would take care of the whole thing and provide work for a large number of the unemployed.
Those are some of the things, Mr. Speaker, which I would suggest to the government that they might do, and do immediately, to relieve the situation. Before this budget passes, for heaven's sake let the government remove some of the grievous inflictions which they have visited upon the trade of Canada with other countries. Let us do something to get rid of our surplus products. Let the government make some move. Do not simply sit still and wait for something to turn up, because it usually does not turn up.
This government has got a great deal of credit for the courage which its leader possesses. Let him exhibit some of that courage now and take a bold step as other countries have done; for the benefit of the taxpayers of this country. If he does that, not only will it help to relieve the situation, but it will save $15,000,000 or $18,000,000 for bonusing, which this government are going to pay out of the treasury, which apparently they consider inexhaustible. We deny our people the right to trade by imposing excessive tariffs, and then in order to provide some compensation for those whom trade restrictions hit the hardest the government dips into the treasury to give a hand-out to those people in order to square things. It cannot be done. In the long run it will mean that we shall not simply be standing on the brink of an abyss, but that we shall go right over unless

drastic action is taken. I say to the government, let them take action, and so far as I am concerned they may depend upon my support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
at the outset may I join with hon. members who have preceded me in congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) upon the lucid manner in which he presented the budget. I agree with hon. members opposite that the minister did not present a very popular budget; in fact there are many points in it which I do not like. At the present time however this government is not looking for votes, and consequently this is not a vote catching budget. It was framed to meet realities, not imaginations.
I followed with a great deal of interest the remarks of the previous speaker, the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) and1 also those of the chief opposition critic, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). After listening to the remarks of these hon. members I am prompted, in all kindness, to class them as listless diatribes, with more heat than light.
Certainly the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth made a very clever legal analysis of the budget, an analysis of which only a high priced corporation lawyer like the hon. member would be capable. I believe I would not. be unfair to him if I said that ten minutes after the close of his remarks he could have risen to his feet and made just as good a speech in favour of the budget, if he were honest with himself, with as much sincerity. All down the line we have been damned for our tariff proposals. Coming from western Canada I am not one who particularly favours tariffs. I have always felt that a low or medium tariff would be in the best interests of Canada as a whole. I realize that east is east and west is west, and what will make a meal for the east will starve the west to death. But, Mr. Speaker, Canada is not made up merely of the sum of its provinces; it is something greater than that. We from the west have to make sacrifices, the same as those in other parts of Canada, for the good of the body politic. That we are doing, and doing cheerfully.
The hon. member for West Edmonton was not quite so critical as the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth. Of course he talked trade and tariffs, money inflation, gold standard, and touched upon all other subjects to the discussion of which we have been listening for weeks. In view of the economic conditions obtaining in Canada to-day, I am sometimes convinced that we need a human standard

The Budget-Mr. Stitt (Nelson)
more than a gold standard. How we are going to bring about that human standard I am not at the moment prepared to suggest. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth criticized at length the deficits on the Canadian National Railways. I believe there has been sufficient evidence adduced in the house to show that the Canadian National is not the only railway system suffering from deficits. Practically all of the greater railways in the United States are in the hands of receivers. The New York Central, one of the best and, in the past, most prosperous railways of the United States is to-day, in that position. For that reason I do not know why the hon. member felt justified in criticizing so severely the Canadian National system. It is simply a victim of conditions, that is all.
With his criticism of the pensions provision in the budget I find myself very much in agreement. I do not think it is necessary to take this crack at pensioners in the civil service. I believe there are other avenues of escape and other sources of revenue which might be explored. What is the position of these pensioners working in the service? When war broke out and Canada threw in her lot with the motherland, two things were asked for, namely men and money. We may picture two chaps, probably chums, one with a good job and the other with one not quite as good. One of these chaps enlists and in due time goes to France. He may come back all knocked to pieces, with a leg off, his nerves shattered and unable to resume his former vocation. The other fellow did not enlist, but stayed at home, and to make his contribution purchased bonds. The point I wish to make is this: We talk a good deal about the sanctity of contracts. If contracts are to be honoured, then, the promise made to the man who went to France is just as sacred as that made to the man who bought the bond. I think the government is ill advised in taking the step outlined in the budget. If it were going to stop there, it would not be so bad. However we have no assurance that provincial governments will not follow suit. Then, industries throughout the country will take similar action, and the first thing we know we will have a general condition as a result of the example set by the government.
If the government feels that returned soldiers should make a further contribution, and if it can be shown to those soldiers that they ought to help meet a national emergency, they will cheerfully make their contribution. But they want fair play. They do not want the government to take money from one branch of the service and let the rest go. We should not take it from the man who
went to France, and not touch the chap who stayed home, slept in a feather bed and had three square meals a day. If it is necessary to assess returned soldiers, I believe it will be much fairer to make a five per cent assessment on pensions up to S50, and ten per cent over that, such assessment to apply throughout the whole pension list. If that action were taken I do not believe there would be a squeal from returned soldiers. They are never very far behind when contributions are necessary.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth has criticised the government because of the falling off in trade and read many figures and statistics to prove his contention. I do not believe the people of Canada are very much interested in the trade figures for the last five years. They want to know what is happening to-day and what is going to happen to-morrow. That is what they are interested in. It must have been most disconcerting to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth when, picking up the Ottawa Citizen the morning after he made that great speech, he read on the first page the following article:
Canada's foreign trade more stable than other nations. Decrease in export trade from 1931 to 1932 only 18-4 per cent, while that of the United Kingdom 20-7 per cent, United States 27-8 per cent, Germany 33-9 per cent, France 37-9 per cent and Austria 41 per cent.
That looks as though we are not the only country in the world which has suffered a loss in trade. I 'think those figures are very interesting in view of the statements that have been made by speaker after speaker from the other side of the house. From start to finish 'their arguments have been based on the assumption that the only country suffering from this depression is the Dominion of Canada.
Now I should like to say a word with regard to the government gamble in wheat, out of which the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth sought to make a good deal of capital. The hon. member damned this government for taking a flier in wheat, as he termed it. Just what do some people in western Canada who are closely in touch with the wheat situation think about that government gamble in wheat? I would not be unfair to the hon. member for Shelbume-Yar-mouth, I think, if I were to say that these men in the west have forgotten more about wheat than he will probably ever know. I have a statement before me made by Professor Swanson of the university of Saskatchewan. This gentleman does not need to be introduced to members of this house; he is one of the best informed men in western
3696	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Stitt (Nelson)
Canada as well * as one of our leading economists. Professor Swanson says that western Canada was saved from economic collapse by the action of the Dominion government in entering the Winnipeg grain market to buy futures at a time when heavy deliveries from western farms were pressing on the market. I think 'the people of the west will be prepared to accept the judgment of Professor Swanson in preference to that of the hon. member far Shelbume-Yarmouth in this connection.
Then the hon. member went on to the stabilization fund, which is designed to help the agriculturists in western 'Canada who are so sorely in need of help at this time. I do not need to deal with the condition of that industry; every western member at least knows full well just what those people are facing to-day. The hon. gentleman damned the government for granting this bonus, as he called it. Again I would quote the opinion of a western man whose judgment I think should carry some weight in this house, and before reading his words may I say that he is not a supporter of the political party on this side of the house. I refer to the lieutenant-governor of Manitoba, who is a very strong Liberal, and who has farmed and raised cattle all his life in western Canada. Lieutenant-Governor J. D. McGregor is reported as having said:
The dawn of a brighter day for the western farmer as tile result of the Rhodes agricultural stabilization fund was predicted by His Honour the Lieutenant-Governor. J. D. McGregor, at the animal meeting of the agricultural bureau of the Winnipeg board of trade-
He goes on further to say:
I am sure we are on the upturn . . . because of the fact that we are getting into the British market on a better basis. It will give an impetus to the marketing of a lot of our products. There is a possibility also of entry into United States markets, but there is no doubt that the British market is our market if we can cater to it.
I think that statement pretty well disposes of the arguments of the hon. member for Sheilburne-Yarmouth.
I do not intend to follow the diatribes of those two hon. gentlemen at greater length; I am going to devote the remainder of the time at my disposal to the discussion of matters that particularly concern my own constituency. Two weeks ago I had no intention of speaking during this debate, but one day the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) made a vicious attack on the Hudson Bay railway, and I have never been backward in my support of that enterprise.
[Mr. B. M. Stitt-1
I have nothing against any hon. member opposite, but the hon. member for North Waterloo is one of those hon. gentlemen whom I like very much. I like his delivery; I like his attitude in debate, but I must say that I thought it was unfair of him to attack this project at this time. The Hudson Bay railway and the port of Churchill are just being put into operation this year. Previously that road has not been open for traffic; there was a dead line at mile 412, and Churchill is mile 511. If you wanted to get a passenger or a package of freight to Churchill you almost had to go down on your knees to some official in order to get a special permit. You do not hear us damning the government for the Prescott elevator which cost $10,000,000, or for the Montreal bridge which cost $19,000,000. Right in the budget the minister was forced to take $26,000,000 from the active column and transfer it to the nonactive column, simply because these harbours are not paying any return on the investment. Why then do these eastern members pick out this particular project and damn it all the time? I would say to my hon. friend that this is no time for this narrow, picayune sectionalism and provincialism. If this country is to become great there must be the heartiest cooperation between all parts of the country. I sincerely hope I have heard the last of this sort of thing in this house. Give this road a chance.

I will add to the foregoing statement the opinions of some men who know what they are talking about. They are opinions that carry more weight than those of gentlemen who sit behind mohogany desks in the old country and set these rates-men who would have a good deal of trouble finding Hudson bay on the map, to say nothing of having any information about it. I will give the opinion of Captain Bernier, an explorer who spent almost a quarter of a century in the northern waters and who knows the Hudson strait and bay probably better than any other man in the world. What does he say? This is the evidence which he gave before the Senate investigating committee:
The Hudson bay and strait are open to navigation the year around, but as far as the strait is concerned icebergs block the way in places according to where the current into or out of the bay drives them. With wireless stations established so that ships could be directed in their course the Hudson bay ports would rank amongst the most important on the continent, owing to the very appreciable difference in distance to Europe compared with that of other ports.
Radio stations and other aids to navigation have been installed and it is now admitted by all shipmasters who have been there to be one of the most foolproof routes in the world. I talk to almost every captain who has sailed into Churchill in the last two years, men who have sailed the seven seas and been all over the world, and every one of them says, without hesitation, "Mr. Stitt, we would much rather go into Churchill than into Montreal, any day." So that it does not lie in the mouths of eastern members to condemn the route before it has been given a fair chance to make good.
I hope that this year the government will see fit to declare the port officially open, and that some sort of celebration will be held there worthy of a route which is going to mean so much to the farmers of western Canada. We who are behind this route, who have given our time and money to bring the project to a successful conclusion, are going to make it our business to see that it gets a fair 53719-234
chance. We are going to tolerate no shenanigans or monkey business from anyone. I do not mean by that that either this government or any member of it has made any attempts at monkey business. I will say for the Minister of Railways that he has cheerfully done everything that any man could be expected to do to make the route a success, notwithstanding adverse criticism; and I can assure the house that had he failed in that respect at any time it would not have been long before I would have got on my feet and told him about it.
This route is being thrown open for business this year. It is still under the control of the Department of Railways and Canals and is in no way connected with the Canadian National Railways. This railroad runs through my constituency and I know a great deal about the territory it serves. This is one of the richest undeveloped pieces of territory in the world to-day. There are 178,000 square miles of virgin territory adjacent to this line, sixty peT cent of which is known to be mineralized. Only two per cent of that area has been prospected, yet we have one of the largest producing mines in the world at Flin Flon, a mine turning out $40,000 of new wealth every day. This development would not have been possible had the Hudson Bay railway not been constructed. Prospecting and exploration work is going on at a dozen different points and new gold finds are being made almost monthly. I hazard the guess that within the next two years there will be ten producing gold mines in that district turning out at least $15,000,000 to $20,000,000 of gold per year.
There are millions and millions of cords of black spruce, the finest pulpwood in the world, not to mention the millions of horsepower still undeveloped. There are other mineral resources besides gold as well as great fishing resources, despite reports to the contrary. I should like to see a proper organization installed as quickly as possible to handle this railroad. An operating superintendent who knows railroading from the ground up should be placed in charge. At the present moment a construction engineer is operating this line. I have no criticism to make of this man as a construction engineer because he is very honest and efficient in that line but we have reached the stage where we are going to put on long pants and a proper organization should be provided. If possible, a new divisional point should be made at The Pas. At the present time there are 772 miles of railroad running out of The Pas. There is the Canadian National line from Hudson Bay Junction to The Pas, the Hudson Bay



The Budget-Mr. Stitt (Nelson)
railway from The Pas to Churchill, the Canadian National line from The Pas to Flin Flon and the Canadian National line from The Pas to Sherritt Gordon Mines on lake Kississing, in all a total of 772 miles. This mileage is the average mileage covered by division points throughout the Canadian National system. With a new divisional point having an operating superintendent in charge, a colonization department could be organized. There are thousands of acres of the finest agricultural land in the world adjoining this railroad and no attempt has been made to tell people about it. The operating superintendent could organize a traffic department which could go out after new business for this road. One of the greatest difficulties facing this road is the fact that it is not connected with the Canadian National Railways although owned by this government. The Canadian National station agents throughout the west at points which this road could serve well and profitably go out of their way to route grain to Fort William or Port Arthur rather than to Churchill over the Hudson Bay railway. They do this because they get no credit for any new business they may obtain for the Hudson Bay line whereas they do get credit for new business obtained for the Canadian National Railways. If this road is going to be given a chance a new divisional point should be created with an operating superintendent in charge.
It is hoped that we will be able to have an official opening of the port this year. If that does take place I hope that as many members of this parliament as possible will attend. I can assure hon. members, especially those from the east, that they will have their eyes opened. A couple of years ago the Canadian chamber of commerce made a trip to Churchill in a special train. I can recall the fur coats and other heavy wearing apparel which they brought along but after their arrival at Churchill they found the weather so warm that the heavy coats were soon placed back in the cars. It was a bright sunny day, just the kind of day you get here in July. We have that kind of weather for almost six months in the year. It is true we have extreme cold and heavy snow storms, but such weather is to be expected in any country bordering on the Arctic. Personally I prefer that kind of weather to the so-called climate you have here. We at least know that we will have winter weather during the winter season. On behalf of The Pas and the north country I extend a most hearty invitation to all members to pay us a visit. They will be sure of a welcome such as only true northerners know how to extend.
