subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first take this opportunity of offering my congratulations to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) for the very complete and businesslike statement which he presented to the house and the country in his budget speech of March 21. In my opinion it gives to the ordinary person a very clear and vivid picture of the financial, condition of the country. It is a statement which should be easily understood, but if not, at least the application of its provisions will I think be readily felt by all. The addition of 8156,000,000 to our national debt should bring home to every citizen the fact that in spite of her great natural wealth, and her virile man power, Canada, under our present financial

The Budget-Mr. Lucas
system, is fast building up a colossal interestbearing debt which if not properly dealt with will eventually drag us down to ruin.
Perhaps one of the bright spots in the budget may be found in the first part of the minister's speech where under the heading, a short review of world economic conditions, he points out that a world financial storm of unprecedented severity first started in Austria, passed from one country to another, finally reaching the United States, which, with its huge gold reserves, had been thought to be impregnable. But the world has recently witnessed the financial debacle which took place in that country, and many are coming to realize that after all gold is not real wealth. Now, however, that the last stronghold has been bombarded and compelled to yield, it may bring home to the people of the world the fact that the financial policies of the past have proved themselves totally inadequate to meet present day conditions, and also that the men who have guided and directed those policies will either have to change their views or give way to men with a clearer vision of the new world in which we live, a world endowed with great wealth, with plenty for all who are ready and willing to work and play their part in society, or else carry on as we are doing, and be dragged down into the bog of misery and despair. The choice, Mr. Speaker, will have to be made and made quickly, for to quote the words of the Minister of Finance in introducing his budget, "Events are moving rapidly, driven by the urge of economic necessity."
Under our present financial system the object of every minister of finance is to balance his budget, a very laudable thing to do if it can be done without entailing too much sacrifice on the pant of the masses of the people. But with a total expenditure of approximately
8418,000.0000, only 8145,000,000 or roughly 35 per cent, of which is controllable expenditure, and with a total deficit of $156,000,000, if we are to balance the budget through economy alone we would have to wipe out all salaries and all services to the people, together with all upkeep of ou-r public works and public buildings, and on top of that find another $11,000,000. Ooe realizes then how absurd the argument becomes Yet we have such bodies as the Montreal board of trade circularizing the members of the House of Commons. advocating the cutting down of expenditures in order to balance the budget. A banker from the same city is also reported on the front page of the Ottawa Citizen, on March 23 last, as saying in regard to the present budget that the only disappointment in the
budget speech is a lack of a serious effort to reduce expenditures. I wonder just what services and expenditures these men would have us cut out. Or do they mean that interest charges, which is by far the largest item in our uncontrollable expenditure, should also be cut?
A careful perusal of the finances of the country shows that while the government have been making heroic efforts to reduce controllable expenditure by the reduction of salaries and services, and so forth, any savings which have been made in this direction have been largely offset by an increase in interest charges. For instance, at page 3223 of Hansard the Minister of Finance makes the following statement:
It is proposed therefore that the original allotments to departments of the votes for controllable services should, when supply is released in the new fiscal year, be so modified that ten per cent of the total, or approximately $14,000,000, will be withheld.
It will be noted that while $14,000,000 is thus to be saved during the coming year, on top of the cuts already made, our interest on the national debt inoreased last year by $13,-
820,000,	or almost all of the saving to be made. It will be seen therefore that while we sacrifice human values, that sacrifice goes to compensate the owners of so-called wealth. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is not the cost of salaries and services that is strangling the people to-day, but our ever-increasing debts and interest charges, the burden of which has been increased tremendously during the past few years by the drastic fall in the price level, thus lessening our ability to pay.
Coming to the budget itself, I should like to deal for a few minutes with some of its provisions. The minister in his budget speech referred to debts and interest. As is well known, this question is now before the banking and commerce committee, and it is to be hoped that when that committee makes its report to the house, constructive suggestions will be offered which will give a lead in dealing with this vexed question. I should like to point out, however, that the figures so far disclosed show debts so enormous that it is hopeless to think of paying them in full. The figures given for dominion, provincial and municipal governments, direct and guaranteed alone show the staggering sum of $6,539,728,053, and when one adds to this corporation obligations other than those guaranteed by government, farm and urban mortgages and private debts amounting to many more billions of dollars, and when one realizes that on top of this our ability to pay has been lessened by fifty per cent or more through
The Budget-Mr. Lucas

the drastic fall in price levels, one then begins to realize the tremendous burden which is dragging us down and commences to see the cause of our present predicament. The proposal to lower interest rates is a step in the right direction but the reduction should be made worth while. However it is not only on savings deposits that interest rates should be reduced, but on bank, mortgage and other forms of debts upon which rates of interest are far too high.
Next we have reference to the conversion loan. By lowering interest charges the minister believes substantial savings can be made to the public treasury. I hope so. I see no reason why Canada should not follow the lead given by Great Britain and Australia, and if necessary make the conversion compulsory. This is no time to quibble with these matters. From all accounts Australia was in a worse financial condition than Canada, but she tackled this problem in a courageous manner. The economy was not made to fall only on the civil servants, wage earners and poorer class of employees. Australian holders of public securities were asked to accept a cut of twenty-two and a half per cent in interest rates, and the interest rates on mortgages were also cut by that figure.
While I heartily agree in principle with sanctity of contracts, I cannot for the life of me see why a contract with a bondholder should be considered any more sacred than a contract to compensate returned soldiers for disabilities received while fighting in defence of our country. Had it not been for these men who were so ready and willing to offer their lives, if need be, bondholders might have found themselves with something of very little valum May I ask if a government employee holding government securities will have his salary reduced by the amount of interest he receives? If not, why not? Why distinguish between pension payments and interest payments? If I might quote a few lines from the chronicle of the Pilgrim Fathers-
It wonderfully encourages men in their duties when they see the burden equally borne.
I will say this, however, that there are pensioners drawing one hundred per cent disability pension and holding jobs requiring one hundred per cent efficiency. I believe this should not be allowed. There can and should be adjustments in such cases, but lower paid men should not be penalized.
Next we have the proposed agricultural stabilization fund to apply to certain agri-

cultural and fish products. May I congratulate the government upon taking this step, which is at least a partial recognition of some of the handicaps under which the farmer has laboured? But, Mr. Speaker, those steps should have been taken long ago. If it is good for certain products, why should it not be applied to all? Because if there is one thing which has been strangling the trade of Canada it has been the disparity in exchange against our goods in British and foreign countries, the currencies of which have been depreciated so much more than our own. In regard to the present proposal, however, it remains to be seen whether the producer or the exporter receives the benefit. I am disappointed that the government has not taken any steps to set up an agricultural export marketing board, about which we heard so much last year. Had this board been properly constituted, and had it been given complete jurisdiction over exports, over shipping, and so on, there is no doubt that the producer would receive full value from the stabilization fund. It is hard to estimate the number of millions of dollars our farmers have lost through the disparity in exchange, and had the farmer benefited, as he should have done, this benefit would have been reflected in an improvement in all lines of business.
The reduction in the value of the pound from $4.40 to $4.25 for duty purposes is another step in the right direction. Again, however, it does not go far enough. The whole step should have been taken last year when the conference agreements were consummated, if we were to derive any real benefit from those agreements. I wish to commend the government upon the assistance it gave to the cooperative wheat pools, and for its efforts to stabilize the price of wheat. Again may I say, however, that much more effective assistance would have been given by bringing our dollar to a parity with sterling, which action would have helped not only agriculture but every other industry in the country. How can our farmers compete against those of countries which have tied their currency to sterling? Australia and New Zealand currency have even gone lower than sterling. In the last issue of the Commercial Intelligence Journal dated March 25, and issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce I find the following at page 419:
Not taking into consideration the acreage bonus which farmers anticipate, growers have recently been receiving from 2s. to 2s. 6d. per bushel of sixty pounds, in Australian currency, for wheat delivered at country railway stations, the disparity being the freight distance to the seaboard.

The Budget-Mr. Lucas
Taking the minimum price of two shillings, it would equal 48 cents per bushel net to the Australian farmer, compared to 30 cents or under for our Canadian western farmer. Some hon. members who preceded me in this debate, speaking on this question, have when making comparisons converted Australian currency into Canadian currency. But may I say that the Australian farmer does not pay his debts in Canadian currency; therefore their argument falls to the ground.
The increase in the income tax is to be commended. Coming on top of the increase of last year it is very substantial, but there is still room for further increases, especially in the higher incomes. I am pleased to note that my suggestions of last year when dealing with taxation in regard to bearer bonds have been adopted, and I am confident this should realize a substantial amount of revenue.
The two cents a pound tax on sugar is in my opinion excessive, and will place a tremendous burden on the already overtaxed householder. The poor man with the large family is the one who will be hit hardest, and our farmers in the west who are struggling to make a living, and the good housewives who try to store up some of the wild fruit to be used by the family during the long winter months, will find it more difficult.
The removal of the exempted list under the sales tax is particularly bad at this time, as it will only tend to lower the standard of living of a great mass of the people, when as a matter of fact what is needed is an increased standard of living so that the great body of people who exist on a mere living wage, or less, may be enabled to consume more of the surplus goods on hand, and thus create a demand, which would again set our factories running and relieve the unemployment burden which is weighing so heavily upon us all.
In fact, Mr. Speaker our action reminds me of the following lines in the Church of England prayer book:
We have left undone those things which we ought to have done, and we have done those things which we ought not to have done, and there is no health in us.
Certainly there is no health in our economic life to-day.
I now come to what I consider by far the most important announcement in the budget, namely the appointment of a royal commission to study the organization and working of our entire banking and monetary system, to consider the arguments for and against a central banking institution, and to make recommendations for revising or supplementing our existing
banking and monetary legislation. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the future happiness and prosperity of the people of this dominion, for at least some time to come, will depend largely on the outcome of this investigation, and the success or failure of this commission will depend wholly on the type of men selected. If the government appoints men of the old school, with the orthodox bankers' viewpoint they might just as well save the country the expense of such a commission. If the world is to be saved from the catastrophe which is now facing it, far-reaching changes will have to be adopted in connection with our banking and monetary	policies.	One	of the greattroubles in the past has been that the people have been kept in ignorance in regard to monetary problems and the intricacies of finance. In	support of	that	statement Ishould like	to	quote a	short	passage from
Norman Angell's book, The Unseen Assassins, at page 143:
We deem	it	necessary	to let our scholars
know about the structure of the earth, its movements round the sun, facts in geography, botany, zoology, something of the stories of kings and queens, snatches of dead languages, and much else, but in all that strange medley of information not one word, from the day that he enters school to the day he leaves, about the most indispensable, the most powerful and the most frequently used of all the devices of our daily lives: the money in our pockets and in our banks, the thing about which-or about matters intimately related to it-we are all of us in some measure called upon to make vital and far-reaching decisions, decisions of _ public policy which affect enormously the distribution of wealth and the fives of millions. Abiput that, we are, speaking broadly, taught nothing whatsoever. The thing which, of all things in human society, concerns us most insistently every day, almost every hour of our fives, and aboxit which man has made some of his worst mistakes and developed his worst understandings-something which has grown into an elaborate system and around which our whole civilization rotates-is something which our popular education completely neglects.
As this quotation points out, the average citizen has been taught little or nothing about monetary matters, and in the past a tendency developed to place our financiers and bankers upon a pedestal surrounded by a veil of mystery, behind which it was considered the rankest kind of sacrilege for the average citizen to attempt to penetrate. But, Mr. Speaker, the happenings of the last few years have disillusioned many people; they have discovered that these men were far overrated and that these so called pillars of finance, upon whom they depended, after all were mere men of clay. The crisis through which we are passing, in my opinion, is purely monetary in character. Other adjustments will have to be
The Budget-Mr. Lucas

made, but they will all prove futile unless we tackle the root cause of the disease and find a remedy for it. I am supported in that statement by an article appearing in the financial column of the Toronto Saturday Night, a publication printed in one of the financial centres of the east. Under date of January 7 Saturday Night has this to say:
The immediate cause of this depression (which need never have occurred) was the inadaptability of our monetary and credit systems to latter day requirements and their inability to stand the extreme strains to which they were subjected, notably by the payment of war debts in gold. Though serious unemployment is a product, this depression is a monetary and not an unemployment depression, and solution of our monetary problems will enable the cure of the unemployment evil.
The Liberal party pins its faith largely on a lowering of tariffs as a remedy. I do not ignore the strangling effect of tariffs as they exist throughout the world to-day but, Mr. Speaker, if we are effectively to lower tariffs we must first remove the root cause. Last year the London chamber of commerce appointed a committee of its members to study this question and make a report, which might form a basis for a discussion of the monetary question at the Imperial economic conference held in Ottawa last July. I think those in charge of the conference made a tremendous mistake when they ignored the report and treated this most important question so lightly; one might almost say it was conveniently shelved. If one will take the trouble to read this report and study the names of the men who composed the committee I think it will be agreed at once that they are men of the very highest standing who could not by any stretch of the imagination be accused of being imbued with communistic doctrines. I should like to quote just a few lines from this repent:
The committee, on January 5 last, issued a memorandum, for private circulation, giving its conclusions. These, however, related only to the domestic aspect of the question, and were designed to provide a currency which would rise and fall automatically with business activity, instead of in accordance with the fortuitous influx and efflux of gold.
The following resolution was adopted:
That in the opinion of this council, monetary reform is of outstanding importance. The arrest of progressive deflation is, in their view, the condition precedent to a restoration of world prosperity, and no other measures which may be taken can prove effective substitutes.
The report goes on to say that the problems with which industry and commerce are faced are these:
(i)	To restore and expand the purchasing power of the peoples of the world, without
[Mr. Lueas.l
which unemployment must remain, and defaults, national and individual, must increase.
(ii)	When once a fair price level has been restored, bo eliminate so far as may be practicable, fluctuations in price level due to monetary causes.
I should like hon. members to listen to this next paragraph:
(iii)	To remove the causes which are inducing nations to strangle world trade by tariffs, quotas, exchange restrictions, etc.
In the final summary, speaking of British domestic matters, the report recommends:
The Bank of England should become a central bank pure and simple. The currency should be issued against all commodities, as represented by the eligible commercial bill-i.e., a bill relating to current production and distribution, and not against one commodity, gold, which can be cornered.
Finally the report states:
With full internal purchasing power in the participating countries, none would object to a fair exchange of commodities with other countries. since imports, visible and invisible, would equal exports, visible and invisible, to a corresponding value. (This does not, of course, mean that the exports to an individual country would necessarily equal the imports from it, or vice versa.)
And again:
Excessive tariffs would therefore tend to disappear. Differences between nations in the volume of internal taxation would be a matter of domestic concern to each, and would not cause disequilibrium as between one nation and another.
International money payments, whether in respect of interest or debts, reparations, etc., could only be received in the form of goods or services against which no corresponding export was made by the receiving country.
There are those who state that the members in this corner stand for a system of uncontrolled inflation. I want to deny that charge. What we are opposed to is any controlled or uncontrolled policy of deflation such as we have had in the past few years. When we find that the total amount of bank loans and currency in Canada is approximately $700,000,000 less to-day than it was three years ago it bears out the statement I have just made. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) speaking a few days ago quoted Irving Fisher as saying that we want neither inflation nor deflation but that we should keep the car in the middle of the road. Perhaps I might illustrate this in a more homely way. Let us take a standard quart of milk, with which everyone is familiar. If we add sufficient water to make two quarts we all know what will be the result; we will have twice the quantity but the food value will not be any greater. This might be called inflated milk. If we start again with a standard quart of milk and put it through a

The Budget-Mr. Lucas
process of dehydration we also know what will be the result; finally we will have what is called powdered milk. This might be called deflated milk. If to that powdered milk is added sufficient water to fill the bottle then we will once more have the standard quart of milk with which we started. No one could say that was inflated milk; rather it might be called reflated milk. We would apply this principle to our money problem; this might be called reflation, and the object would be to restore the volume of circulating media to a normal relation to the volume of business to be done. Is there anything unsound in such a proposal?
I venture to predict that a measure of inflation will be adopted at the coming world conference, most likely by depreciating the value of gold in our dollar; but it will be inflation just the same. So long, however, as those in authority feel that they must still tie our -currency to some metal, if we get some measure of inflation that will give some assistance I am sure we shall all appreciate it.
Let us pause and ask ourselves just what is wrong to-day. Has nature failed us? Has man's inventive genius lessened? Has the large percentage of the human race refused to work? Is there any real lack of demand for the necessities and luxuries of life? Have our transportation systems broken down? No, Mr. Speaker, emphatically no. None of these things have failed nor are they seriously at fault, but the one thing money, using that term in its broadest sense, our medium of exchange, has ceased to function properly, to -distribute the goods which we can produce so abundantly; and until the whole monetary system is made to serve mankind, instead of mankind serving money as it is doing at present, I see no hope for a permanent recovery.
Let all the money in the world disappear to-morrow and ask yourself: Would the world be any poorer, so far as the necessities of life are concerned? Money is not wealth, but only a symbol of wealth. I could quote many authorities in support of this statement, but I will not take time to-night to do so. Are we then to starve amidst the greatest plenty the world has ever known? Surely the intelligence of mankind, which through science has conquered and subdued to his commands the superhuman powers of nature, will not now perish because forsooth we cannot find sufficient gold, which is of no value so far as human needs are concerned.
Here may I quote a short passage from one of Professor Soddy's works, The Inversion of Science, at page 13:
What solution have the statesmen to offer? Mr. Baldwin has recently remarked that it is no use our being able to make things if we
cannot sell them, a true deduction from what Ruskin termed mercantile economy, but not a statesman's sentiment. Is there no one now in the state to regulate its bits of paper and metal so that people who can and do make things can buy them? The recent president of the board of education, justifying his betrayal of his trust, remarked, "The grim goddess of finance exercised, as she always must, an inexorable power.'' These utterances show that the ostensible government of this country is not its real government and that^we are in the grip of a money power which will rivet unemployment and war upon society till its doom.
Only a few short years ago the world was gripped in a death struggle, the greatest war ever known in human history, and while those who fought thought they were fighting to end war, we find now, only fourteen years after, almost superhuman efforts being made to avert another conflict. And what is the main cause? Let me quote again from the same work of Professor Soddy, at page 15:
Anticipating somewhat the conclusions to be arrived at, we may define here the cause of war more precisely as due to an accumulation of mutual international indebtedness without any possible method of repayment. Strong nations at once get the weaker into their debt and prefer to extort from them a permanent annual tribute of wealth by way of interest, rather than to allow them to repay the principal and go free. War cannot be abolished till that is rectified.
History records that down through the ages some form of human slavery has always existed, some form of mastership controlled. As our civilization developed, mankind revolted against this form of treatment and a determined effort has been made to free the human race from such tyranny. It may be within the memory of some men in this house when human slavery was abolished on this continent; but while the type of slavery of which we have been accustomed to think has been abolished, another form more subtle, more insidious in its character, has been fastened upon a great majority of the human family. I refer to the financial power that dominates the world. The slave of old had to be clothed, fed and sheltered and could at least sleep from bodily fatigue; but what about the millions of people to-day who, because of the burden of debt, even find it hard to sleep from worry and fear, fear of seeing their life savings disappear, in most cases through no fault of their own, fear of the spectre of want, fear of being thrown upon charity for their subsistence, the fear of thousands of our youths coming out of school, fitted and ready to make their contribution to life but denied the right to work? Let me ask, how long is.this sort of thing to continue?
The Budget-Mr. Lucas

Just as the barons in days gone by wrung from King John that charter of liberty which we prize so highly to-day; just as our forefathers fought and conquered one obstacle after another, to lift mankind to a higher plane; just as science and research have rid the world of that dread spectre of famine and scarcity, so surely we in our day and generation will not hesitate to do our part in ridding the world of that giant octopus money power, wiliich is spreading its tentacles in every direction and dragging the human race down to destruction. I hope and trust therefore that the government will realize the important task which lies ahead of this royal commission which is to be appointed.
Finance has developed to such an extent along with the development of the industrial machine that it has become the very lifeblood, or the air of our business and industrial life. We would not for a moment think of granting to a small group of men the right to control the air about us, which we all need in order to live, and yet we have done that very thing so far as our business and industrial life is concerned; and while this power, granted no doubt unconsciously, has grown up gradually, clothed in a veil of mystery to the average citizen, the disclosures of the past few years have broken the spell and in my opinion the time has come when the people will demand that this money monopoly must be broken and the control returned to the people to whom it rightly belongs.
. Mankind has made tremendous strides in learning how to control and prevent disease, and has long since discarded the belief that pestilence and plagues are an act of God. When he develops the will to do so, man can also prevent unemployment and poverty. Man is no longer the slave but the master of nature, in so far as eliminating the fear of scarcity is concerned; and when he discards the cloak of mystery and superstition which surrounds our economic structure and assumes the control and regulation of finance in all its various phases, in the interests and general wellbeing of all, he will for the first time in history become the real master of his fate, and carry civilization to new heights of achievement in peace and security.
In regal'd to the Liberal amendment, Mr. Speaker, it is nothing but a sweeping condemnation of the government, without offering one constructive suggestion, something which the people are looking for at this time. I am inclined to believe that the people of the country are more interested in a change to a system that would bring some relief to their sufferings than they are in a mere change from

one party to another, which would carry on along very much similar lines.
While we in this coiner of the house recognize that the budget contains certain commendable features, while we recognize that under present world conditions any government in power must face tremendous difficulties and carry heavy responsibilities, yet we feel that we must register our protest against a continuation of the present disastrous policy of deflation. But in doing so we wish to offer something of a constructive character, something which we believe, if put into effect, would go a long way towards relieving the people of the tremendous burden, under which they are at the present time struggling, and also restore that measure of prosperity and happiness which we are all so anxious to bring about.
I therefore beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), the following:
That all the words after "therefor" in the said proposed amendment be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
"Whereas, the present depressed condition of agriculture, industry and of business generally, with its consequent unemployment, is the direct result of fundamental defects in our economic system, accentuated during recent years by the policies of deflation and of credit restriction which have been followed by different governments and financial institutions, and
"Whereas, while it is recognized that the present budget contains certain commendable features, including the proposed appointment of a royal commission to investigate hanking and finance, and a measure of assistance to agriculture, it must also be recognized that it is based in principle upon a continuance of the aforesaid ruinous _ policies of deflation and an increased restriction of purchasing power, and 'Whereas, the continuance of these policies, accompanied as they must be by a constantly increasing burden of debt, recurring budget deficits, and a decrease of purchasing power, and therefore of consumption, must inevitably result in a condition of still greater depression, and increasing unemployment, and
"Whereas, it is imperative, in view of the foregoing facts, that such policies be inaugurated as will have the effect of restoring the price level of agriculture, and other primary products, increasing purchasing power, reducing the burden of interest bearing liabilities, encouraging consumption and raising the standard of living amongst our people;
"Therefore be it resolved, that in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate consideration to the introduction of such measures as may-
"(a) Make available the real credit of the nation through the instrumentality of a national central bank, and render possible the utilization and control of this credit for the legitimate needs of the people of this country;
"(b) Bring about such a degree of controlled inflation as would stabilize the price level of

The Budget-Mr. Davies
our chief commodities at a point where it would bear a reasonable relation to costs of production and to incurred obligations;
"(c) Provide employment and purchasing power to our people, through the above mentioned means, and where necessary, by the direct use of our national credit in the construction of public works of various kinds, and in other ways which might be suggested including the construction of houses, etc.;
"(d) Ensure a more equitable distribution of the national income through well considered methods of taxation, and the legislative control of interest, profits and investment;
"(e) Nationalize our insurance systems, including the establishment of such systems of social insurance as may be necessary for the protection and well being of our people."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been said that the path of popularity and the path of duty do not always coincide, and I feel sure that if the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) was not fully acquainted with all the implications of that aphorism before he took over his present portfolio, he has become convinced of its truth since that time. I am sure all hon. members of this house are fully appreciative of the fact that a most difficult task was placed in the hands of the Minister of Finance, but I think hon. members, on this side at least, will acknowledge that that task has been done very well. I have not been a member of this house for any great period of time, but I have been here long enough to know that the character of its deliberations are both varied and variegated. Sometimes its deliberations are most serious; at other times they are interesting-not only because they are serious-but also because, unfortunately, they are both amusing and tragic. It is because I think that the address delivered on March 24, by the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) comes within the four corners of these qualifications, and in particular within the confines of the latter two, that I hope to make reference to it, in some measure of detail, before I conclude.
In passing may I say that as I sat and listened to the address of the hon. member I could not help but think of the similarity which existed between him and his speech and Christopher Columbus and his voyage westward. Hon. members will recall that Christopher Columbus, after taking the blessing of the Queen of Spain-and incidentally all her money-started out on his voyage. When he started out, he did not know where he was going; when he got there, he did not know where he was, and when he came back, he did not know where he had been. So it was, it seems to me, with the speech of the hon.
member for Shelbume-Yarmouth. When he started out, it was obvious, at least to all hon. members on this side of the house, that he did not know where he was going. When he got to where he did not know he was going, it was equally obvious that he did not know where he was, and when he came back home from where he did not know where he was going to, it was again obvious that he did not know where he had been.
May I refer for a moment or two to that portion of the budget in which the Minister of Finance announced the appointment of a royal commission to make a study of the financial structure of the country. I think the minister is to be particularly commended for having decided to do this, because unquestionably, as many hon. members have stated, this matter goes to the root of our present difficulties. There is one question which I hope this royal commission will study in detail, and that is the relationship between our present monetary base and unemployment. My knowledge, I must confess, is very elementary, but I am convinced that some relationship does exist between these two matters. A great many different economists have been quoted in this chamber and strangely enough, there is just one thing upon which they all agree, namely that the present depression which started with the financial collapse of 1929, is substantially nothing more nor less than a breaking down of the medium of exchange. Upon different occasions hon. members sitting to the extreme left of Your Honour have referred to the results. They have stated, not infrequently, that in the world to-day we find want in the midst of plenty. May I say to them that if hon. members on this side do not express the same opinions to the same degree it is not because they do not recognize that such conditions exist throughout the world. On the contrary, may I venture the opinion that a good many more grey hairs have been added to the heads of hon. members sitting on this side of the chamber, who perhaps have talked less about these things, than to the heads of those who have done much more talking; for we on this side of the house have had the misfortune-it is the good fortune of the country-to be charged with the responsibilities of government in these distressing times.
I should like to refer particularly to the conditions which exist in the United States, because I think that country provides an apt illustration of exactly what our difficulties are and fortifies me in my belief as to the real
The Budget-Mr. Davies

difficulty. While the diagnosis may not be very difficult, unquestionably the cure is.
Hon. members who are acquainted with United States statistics will perhaps recall that the export trade of the United States-I speak from memory, but I think I am right-is approximately only ten per cent of its total production. Therefore it must be obvious to all that the greatest market for that country is its home market. The United States has practically everything it needs and it has the possibility of being the most independent country of any in the world; nature has endowed it with everything. They grow oranges in California, bananas in Florida; they have huge coal mines in Vermont and Pennsylvania; they have iron ore in tremendous quantities in Minnesota; they have oil in Oklahoma, Texas and California, and they have the great wheat fields of the plains of the middle west. It is not sufficient, therefore, for the United States, having regard to the fact that its exports are only ten per cent of its total production, to say: WTell, quotas and tariffs have quenched our export trade; because, after all, the greatest market for its products is within its own boundaries. Nobody will deny that the productivity of the great republic to the south of us is ample to take care of all its needs; nobody will deny that in that population of 120,000,000 there are many more millions of wants waiting to be satisfied. It would seem therefore safe to draw the conclusion that the only reason the productivity of that country cannot be taken advantage of by those who wish to do so is that the means of exchange has broken down-she has an antediluvian system of exchange. This brings us logically to the money question.
Is there anything more pitiful than the conditions to which the breakdown in the exchange situation has brought us? Is there anything more pitiful than an honest man, with a wife and family, who wants a job, a chance to earn an honest day's living, and cannot get it? That is the problem which faces all governments throughout the world, and the present civilization has to solve it or else in the course of time nothing but anarchy can result.
I should like to pause for a moment to ask what the purpose of government is. I must confess very frankly that until I decided to say a few words in this debate, I had not stopped to consider the question of the purpose of government. But I think all hon. members will agree that the purpose of government, whether here or elsewhere, should be to create an ideal state. Many hon. members may disagree as to what that is. I have been

in the house for a sufficient length of time to know that the idea of the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) of an ideal state might be one which did not have any tariffs. The idea of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) as to an ideal state might well be one which did not have a criminal code, or if it had to have one, it would be one in which section 98 was deleted. I do not think I would be unkind in saying that possibly the idea of the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) of an ideal state would be one where "someone would do something sensible." I see the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not in his seat, but I imagine he might have an entirely different conception of an ideal state. He might think it would be one which would be a broad plain, completely flat, in order that there might be no "valley of humiliation" in it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think perhaps, economically speaking, we might all agree an ideal state conceivably might be one in which there would be more jobs than men to fill them and in which every honest day's work would bring an honest day's pay. Out of such a definition it would naturally follow that such a state would have a reasonably stable price level.
The next question I should like to consider is what hope we have of achieving an objective of that nature with our money based on gold. I frankly confess I cannot see much hope in the light of my present knowledge. May I give my reasons? In the first place, if gold is to be the basis of our currency, it necessarily follows that it determines the amount of currency that is issued, whether it be metal coins or notes, subject only to slight qualification. Unfortunately the gold production of the world is more or less static, but business is progressive. Science, invention and discovery are improving the means of production, and the needs of the people increase as new wants are created. But the production

The Budget-Mr. Davies
of gold has no relation whatsoever to the goods that have to be handed over and the services that have to be rendered. This is clearly illustrated if one looks at the present situation in Canada. We have on hand approximately $78,000,000 of gold and about $175,000,000 of dominion notes outstanding. In February the deposits in our savings accounts amounted to about $1,397,000,000, and current bank loans were approximately $1,000,000,000. Theoretically those loans would cancel the deposits, but again, theoretically speaking, everybody with a savings account is entitled to draw his money out if he wants it, and if so, he is entitled to demand dominion notes. If we were on the gold standard -we are not-he would be entitled to demand gold for his dominion notes, and we therefore have this huge credit structure built up on merely $78,000,000 worth of gold, an amount which bears no relation whatsoever to the structure.
My second complaint against gold as a money basis is that no provision is made in gold for the retention of the national income when debts are being deflated. May I make myself a little clearer on this point? After all, every time a bank loan is repaid, money- purchasing power-is taken out of circulation unless at the same time as that bank loan is repaid, a new loan is taken out. That is a matter which I think we should all recognize; we can follow it through very simply. Under our present arrangement, let us suppose that the supply of the products of an industry is too great and that the demand is not there. What happens? The industry lays off men, who join the ranks of the unemployed and thus lose their purchasing power. In losing their purchasing power, they are no longer taxpayers; they even have to be kept by the state and become a charge on all other taxpayers. Their unemployment-no purchasing power-further aggravates the situation. That is what is happening now; it has happened all along; it has happened in previous depressions. It explains business cycles, because when debts have to be paid out of earnings, without a new loan being made, the process of deflation is started.
What does the policy of "easy money" mean? I look forward to such a policy. I was glad to hear the Minister of Finance say that the government was prepared to reduce the interest rate on postal savings, but while the banks have been talking for some time of reducing their interest rate on deposits, it is hardly possible they will do so unless there is cooperation throughout the country. The provinces must reduce interest rates on their
deposits because it is unreasonable to expect the banks to reduce their interest rates while provinces, which are in competition in taking public funds into their savings, do not do so also. If this adjustment is not forthcoming in the not distant future and if there does not appear to be cooperation between these various bodies, I hope the Minister of Finance will take advantage of the provisions relating to "peace, order and good government" so as to bring about that cooperation. Why do we look forward to this policy of easy money? Is it only because we think w-e will be able to pay our debts more easily, or is it not also because it will be easier for us to go into debt? After all, every credit is a debt; is it not a fact that we are waiting for somebody to go into debt in order to get business going and thus clear away the depression?
Another objection that I have to gold is this. With gold as a basis of money, having regard to our present available supplies, it seems to me it is dependent upon a contracting and expanding body of unemployed labour for stabilizing the price level. What I mean is this: under- the gold standard, if the supply of the products of industry is too great for the demand, men are laid off. It is expected then that production will diminish to some extent, and when it does catch up again, if it does, if we do not run into another cycle of deflation and depression, we expect the men to be reemployed to meet the new demands for production. I should like to spend more time in registering one or two other points in this connection, but I must pass on in order even roughly to cover the field.
It seems to me that with gold as the money base there is only one logical way of solving the problems of a depression or period of deflation, and that is by putting everybody- all the unemployed-to work in the gold mines. I cannot see any other way. I can see ways of relieving the situation, but I cannot see the solution. Let us assume for a minute that all the provinces in Canada had potential gold mines. Then the logical thing to do when a man became unemployed would be to put him to work in a gold mine, to produce the money base. The result would be that Alberta gold would be sent to the Minister of Finance and he could issue new bills against it. That would create new purchasing power, and that is the only way in which he can create it. This in turn would stimulate industry and national income would be maintained. If all the countries of the world had potential gold properties where they could put their unemployed to work the depression would be solved quickly under the gold standard; but they do
The Budget-Mr. Davies

not happen to have them. Our gold mines have been of tremendous benefit to us, but it seems to me that they have not been of the benefit they might have been, because we happen to be a debtor country. What happens at the present time is: that the gold mines of Canada are being entirely supported by the taxpayer's of the country. I am not objecting to this because it is what we have to do; but we are paying the gold mines for the gold they produce and then sending that gold to New York to meet our obligations. The difficulty therefore at present is that all the gold we are producing is not a basis for currency expansion in Canada. Neither is it any good to the United States because she has not used her accumulated gold reserves as a basis of monetary expansion. The work was done in Canada'-this does not 'help the United States.
Now if we can agree that the logical way to solve this depression is to put everybody to work in the gold mines at the production of the metal base of our currency, I think we can reasonably agree, further, that that indicates a weakness in gold alone as a money base, for it is something that is too scarce; it is not plentiful enough, and is not equitably distributed.
A great many suggestions have been offered as to what might be done to patch up gold. The hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) told the house of the revaluation plan of Peter Robertson. Doctor Stephen Leacock has published a little book in which he puts forward a plan which amounts to the same thing. His book is entitled something to this effect: How to solve the depression in six seconds, eradicate it in six minutes, and permanently cure it in six hours. He advocates the reduction of the gold value of the dollar by twenty-five per cent.
Then there is the suggestion of an international banker or economist that gold certificates should be issued by the Bank of International Settlements, and that these gold certificates by treaty should be accepted in all the various countries as gold. They would be loaned out to countries in need of gold reserves. There is also the suggestion that silver should be remonetized. But these suggestions are all practically the same in principle. They all admit the fact that there is not a sufficient quantity of the monetary base in the world. I do not for a moment doubt but that by these various means the price level can be raised1; there is no doubt that it can be. I do not doubt that through bringing about revaluation a reasonable measure of prosperity can be brought back, but so far as producing an ideal state, or a return of permanent prosperity is concerned,

I must confess that I cannot see any very definite hope in that direction through such suggestions. I am afraid we will just be preparing ourselves for another business cycle.
How do my hon. friends in the southeast corner of the house view the situation? They look at it in this way:	Here is a man who
has been working in a boot factory and is now out of work; there are others who need boots. Here is the plant. They say: "This whole thing is a dirty mess. Let the government take it over." I think that is what socialism is. I cannot agree with my hon. friends in the southeast corner in their method by which they would get us out of the depression. They look upon the government, as one writer has called it, as an omnicompetent political chore-boy robot who can accomplish everything. I do not view the function of government in that light. If that form of state socialism was adopted-and that is what they advocate -unless the real causes are got at, would we have anything more than something in the nature of a glorious scheme of national relief?

as well under the present system, and there is no use changing unless your system has something better to offer, and it hasn't. Then my hon. friends in the southeast corner look at the banks. They see the beautiful buildings and the nicely polished brass doors. They see the weekly bank returns showing savings deposits of approximately one and a half billion of dollars, and they say: "Let us nationalize the banks and take the whole thing over; we will fix this thing up." But is that necessary? With our banks nationalized and our bank managers and bank employees directly or indirectly civil servants, would it be easier to lend a dollar to any man than it is under existing conditions? There are only two ways to get purchasing power into the hands of the people; one way is to give it out and get something done; the other way is to hand it out and get nothing done. I firmly believe that under a socialized or nationalized banking system if money would be handed out without any reasonable expectation of its being returned -and I submit that it would not be returned under existing conditions-the final result would be that the banking system would run the state into bankruptcy much quicker than the Canadian National Railways has any possibility of doing.
It seems to me that there is another very substantial defect in what my hon. friends in that corner of the house advance, and that is that it would bring credit into the sphere

The Budget-Mr. Davies
of politics. It would seem to me that that is an evil which above all we should steer clear of. If we are going to have a democracy-and they tell us that under their scheme we would have-and that democracy is going to operate the banks, how could you keep credit out of politics? What would be the consequences?
The question naturally arises, what should be done? It is much easier to see what some of the fundamental causes of our difficulties are than to suggest practical remedies. May I, however, draw the attention of the house to a book recently written in which the writer puts forward a suggestion which I have not heard put forward in this house. I am not in a position to say .that the suggestion is sound, but this writer, who has been studying the question for a great many years, advocates public improvements as a' money base. He says that it would solve the depression and ensure permanent employment by making public improvements the money standard. He would at all times put the unemployed to work on public improvements. He selects public improvements because there is no limit to the public improvements which a nation will want as time advances-roads, bridges, sanitation schemes, cleaning up the slums, and so forth-all of which would raise our standard of living. He would pay for these public improvements with a newly issued money, just as if we had half a billion dollars' worth of gold produced in this country which we did not have to send abroad to pay our debts, and the Minister of Finance would issue new currency when that was delivered to him. He would retire by taxation the currency thus issued at the rate of depreciation. This writer points out that under this scheme unemployment would be done away with. Let us suppose that through technological improvements in industry men would be thrown out of employment; his plan would be to put them to work on public improvements-put them into the production of the money base, just as if we cou'ld put men to work in our gold mines to-day of which we have not sufficient, despite the fact that we are the world's second largest gold producer. In this manner he submits that the purchasing power of the people, in other words the national income, would be retained while debts were being deflated, which unfortunately is not the case at the present time. If one were to compare such a money standard with the gold standard, one might make the comparison first on the basis of redeem-ability. Well, it must be obvious that such 53719-235
a currency would not be redeemable. If the Minister of Finance was presented with a dominion note he could not walk over to the east block, pick off a couple of huge stones and say, "Here is your portion of the public funds." Obviously such a currency would not be redeemable. But, on the other hand is gold redeemable? Gold is only redeemable, it seems to me, so long as you do not ask for it to be redeemed. The essence of its re-deemability is that you do not ask for it. We have seen what happened in the United States, and throughout the world. Once you ask that it be redeemed, you cannot get it.
Then, as to its utility: It would seem desirable, I suppose, that our money should be based upon something which would have some utility-which gold has not. He compares it with gold in this way, by saying, "We mine gold, and put it away in the vault. I doubt if it creates much happiness or raises our standard of living." On the other hand he continues: "With public works as a money standard; as you continually launch your public works program the standard of living of the people would be raised, because they would have utility."
There is one other item I should like to refer to in this connection. I said I hoped that the commission would study the relation between unemployment and money, and our money base in particular. That brings me to express this view: We have been told that the big thing behind our money, that which is of most importance, is "confidence." We have been told, furthermore, that "confidence" is largely dependent upon our ability to meet our foreign debts in the terms of our contract. If that is so, if that is what "confidence" is dependent upon, may we not make further inquiry and see upon what does our ability to meet our foreign debts depend. It seems to me there are only two ways in which foreign debts can be met, one is by the shipment of gold, and the other by the creation of credits in a foreign or creditor country, which is done by the shipment of goods and the performance of services. Otherwise, the only way left open to us to meet foreign debts is to borrow in a creditor country. If this is so it naturally follows that every time one joins the ranks of the unemployed, there is one less working to help establish these foreign credits.
It was the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) who said he did not understand why, when we issued $68,000,000 of dominion notes during war time and had no gold behind them, it was possible that since that time our currency was at a premium over United States funds. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
it is a happy circumstance that in this house, where there is such a great difference of opinion on almost every subject that is brought up for discussion, there should be one thing on which we are unanimous; that is, the manner in which the budget speech was presented to the house. So I should1 like to add my congratulations to those already expressed.
Before dealing with the budget itself I should like to offer some criticisms with regard to some of the speeches that have been made, and to point out the fallacies contained in some of the arguments that have been advanced. While in the main I disagree with the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) there was one remark which he made in opening that I think will be received throughout the country with the same measure of approval that was shown in this house-at least this will be so if the future works of the government give evidence of the new faith that is in them. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
. As we look back over the past year and, indeed, over the past three or four years, many of us are willing to admit that we are much wiser to-day than we were three or four years ago. Many proposals made with great confidence that some suggestion, if accepted, would cure all the ills from which we were suffering, we now realize were mistaken ideas.
That expression was received with a great deal of applause from this side of the house, and my hon. friend added:
My hon. friends opposite seem to think the monopoly of that rests with this side of the house, but I have very definitely in mind innumerable weird suggestions that have come from the other side.
Just at this point let me say to the minister that the policies which have been advocated from this side of the house are not on trial; the policies advocated by the government
53719-235J
during the past two or three years are on trial. Those are the policies that have been weighed in the balance and found wanting. Let us hope, however, that the minister's statement means that the government have recognized that the proposals they made, which were to bring about the salvation of the country, have been found not to have accomplished the end hoped for. Let us hope that his statement means a repudiation of the doctrine of Canada first, as defined by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett); let us hope that it means the repudiation of such doctrines as shutting out the foreigner and making the foreigner pay tribute to the empire, or that red-blooded doctrine enunciated by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion). Let us hope also that it means an end to that long series of letters which, following the election of 1930, the Minister of Trade and Commerce addressed to the people of Canada, and which were published in all newspapers throughout the dominion at public expense.
I wish I had time to readi extensively from this document, which is one of the first if not the first of the letters issued. It is headed and addressed as follows:
Department of Trade and Commerce Ottawa, Canada
To my fellow citizens, in every part of the Dominion:
I should like to quote a few sentences from this letter:
Every year for the past few years Canada has been importing $800,000,000 worth of merchandise that she might just as well have been producing from her own mines, on her own farms or in her own factories. Some things, of course, like raw cotton and raw rubber, she must import. But making due allowance for such items, the fact remains that $800,000,000 of her annual imports have been of a class or kind that she was quite capable of producing for herself.
Then in the next paragraph he goes on to argue that if proper policies were pursued employment would be given directly to 147,527 workers in Canada. It was in order that effect might be given to this policy that during the session of 1930 the government undertook to raise tariffs immediately. A little later another letter appeared, headed with these words: "Remember the Golden Rule."
I think the minister and the country will have to recognize that the golden rule has a very much wider application than has been given it by those who advocated the Canada first, the shut out the foreigner and the make the foreigner pay tribute policies. Finally let us hope that the statement of the minister
The Budget-Mr. Brown

means the repudiation of that famous creed which was presented to us in such an attractive form. Therein lies its danger. Ever since the woman looked upon the forbidden fruit and saw that it was pleasant to the eye, evil has 'been most insidious when presented in a form that was not outwardly repulsive. Sometimes it has worn the garb of innocence; indeed sometimes it was seemingly good. We recognize this in our English speech; we refer to the wolf in sheep's clothing; we speak of Satan arrayed as an angel of light. So this creed, containing as it does many beautiful expressions, nevertheless contains the germ of that disease which has been afflicting the world, that extreme nationalism which has brought our modern civilization to the very brink of the precipice.
This is not the only confession of past error we have had since the opening of this session; we had another from the Prime Minister. When the hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough (Mr. Duff) moved his resolution advocating reciprocity with the United States we were completely astonished to hear the Prime Minister raise his voice in favour of that suggestion. There is no question of what his attitude has been in the past, but when he changes his faith I think he should take his supporters into his confidence so they will not make contrary statements. For example, it would have been well if the right hon. gentleman had taken the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Beaubien) into his confidence before that hon. gentleman issued this long letter to his constituents, in which he said:
Canada may as well make up her mind that she cannot hope for anything like dependable trade arrangements -with the United States. That country, whether it is a Republican or a Democratic administration, and no matter what the political complexion of congress, doesn't propose to buy anything from Canada that it can help; and any arrangements that it can make with Canada of a contrary nature will be a temporary arrangement, subject to withdrawal at congressional caprice.
That is just one paragraph from this letter; it is not at all in agreement with the statement made in this house by the Prime Minister, in the course of which he said that he now favours a reciprocity with the United States. There is no question that in the past the Prime Minister did commit himself to the policy of no trade with the United States except when we could not deal within our own country. Evidently the right hon. gentleman has seen the error of his ways; he has seen the complete breakdown of that policy of extreme nationalism which has been the curse of modern times. It would be more honest if he would candidly admit his error and not try to give the country the im-
I Mr. Brown.]
pression that it was not the principle of reciprocity that he opposed but the form in which it was presented to the people. That is what he tried to tell us in the house when the matter was before us a few weeks ago. Oh no; he did not seem to be opposed to reciprocity, but he did not like the idea of a loose agreement that could be cancelled in a very short time.
I know it is not permissible for me to quote from a former debate in the same session, but we all remember that speech and we remember the reason he gave for his having opposed reciprocity back in 1911. But *that was not the attitude taken by the Conservative party at that time. They opposed reciprocity because they thought they saw in that agreement our entire separation from the British Empire. One of the chief Conservative leaders at that time was the late Sir George Foster, and I want to read the closing words of his speech, delivered in the House of Commons on February 14, 1911, so that the house may see 'the reasons he gave for opposing the reciprocity pact, and also just to what extent his reasons agreed with what the Prime Minister told us a few days ago. Let me quote:
This proposal cuts square across that national ideal, challenges it at every point, will endanger it undoubtedly, may destroy it entirely. Should we not think before we enter into it? Ninety-three millions to the south of us mean it in the way of absorption and hegemony and mean it in no other way, hence these gifts. This proposal cuts our country into sections and at every section bleeds the life blood from it. The well-filled arteries of interprovincial trade will be drained until the whole system grows anaemic and flabby. Do not treat it lightly. The sustained pressure of ninety-three millions to eight millions, the far-reaching effect of business affiliation, the close proximity and constant efflux and influx, the seductions of commercialism, the constant intercourse of business, social and official life, will inevitably weaken the ties of empire and wean the thoughts of our newer generations, if not of ourselves, towards the predominant power, and create new attachments, until like Samson we would arise and would shake ourselves and find that our strength is gone.
I utter the most solemn words I have ever uttered in my life, and I believe them to the very bottom of my heart, that there is danger, and deep danger ahead. This path entered upon leads us away from home to a strange country. I pray, sir, that the full meaning of this first step may sink into the hearts of members of parliament and into the hearts of the people of this country until there shall burst forth a protest of such strength that the steps contemplated will be recalled to the old paths, leading east and west, in and out amongst our own people, converging on the great metropolis of the mother land, and which we may follow without uncertainty and without menace to our national existence.

Good stuff perhaps, but
very different from ryhatt the Prime Minister gave us the other day. Well, the campaign was fought out along those lines. I remember the Manitoba campaign organized by the present member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Rogers), who then had the reputation of being one of the greatest election winners in Canada. At any rate, the campaign was organized by that hon. gentleman, and he brought with him Mr., afterwards Sir Robert Borden and another gentleman who afterwards became a cabinet minister, ito the town of Morden in my constituency. I travelled from my own town to hear them, and I remembeT the dire picture they painted of what would happen to Canada if we entered into that arrangement. I remember (hearing of the 90,000,000 head of cattle that would come from the United State's and graze in our pastures, and of the disastrous consequences that would follow if we yielded to the solicitations that were being put forward. I remember the Conservative candidate at that time, a gentleman who now sits in the other house, telling us after it was over, "We saved Canada". That was the way the campaign was fought and it ended, as other campaigns have ended, by the people responding to the absurd pleas that were made to them. lit was another instance in which, in our judgment, democracy showed its weakness by counting the number of heads instead of taking the quality into consideration.

To many of us, it seems but fitting that a member of the royal family should open a new parliament, with a new government with a clear mandate from the people on a great issue, indicating in no uncertain terms a settled conviction that the Canadian people would consider no trade proposals that menaced, even remotely, their fiscal and national independence, or threatened to lessen the strength of the ties that bind them to the British Empire,-
We remember what we heard a session or two ago about cutting the painter that binds us to those islands across the sea.
-or rendered for a moment more difficult the realization of the hope that lives in all of us for the commercial and organic union of that empire.
Mr. Speaker, the risk was real and the danger imminent. I doubt not that when the proposals to which I have referred were first introduced, they were regarded merely as trade proposals; but when it was ascertained that in their ultimate results they involved the whole future
of Canada, then it was that the national spirit of our people was aroused. I venture to think that the right hon. gentleman who so successfully leads the opposition in this house would not have introduced those proposals if he could have foreseen that there would have arisen around them an agitation, the results of which were so vital to the imperial and national future of the country.
I shall stop there, for I am afraid that if I continue reading from it I may not have time to say all I want to. But that extract shows sufficiently that the opposition of the present Prime Minister to reciprocity in 1911 was not on the ground that the agreement was loose, as he now says; rather, the reason was as indicated in the quotation I have just given.
When I heard the confession of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) that the government's policies had now proved inadequate, I was reminded of another confession I once heard him make, and I wast still more reminded of it as he proceeded with his speech. He once admitted in a burst of candor that when his case was weak he was unusually vigorous in presenting it; in other words, he made up in vigour what he lacked in logic. There were a number of illustrations of that truth in the speech to which we listened the other day. For instance, when ihe turned his guns against the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmoutfa (Mr. Ralston) with regard to stabilization. He tried to prove that the hon. member was inconsistent because in the first place he had condemned the principle involved and then later, as the minister tried to make out, the hon. gentleman had urged the application of the same principle to all exports. But someone on 'this side pointed out that the minister was forgetting that little word "if"-if it was sound. The minister saw he had made a mistake and it was rather amusing to see him floundering about for a while. It reminded me of the only other time I have ever seen Hie minister completely floored, the time he undertook to defend the hon. member for East Simeoe [DOT] (Mr. Thompson) when the Vigilant matter was before the house. That was one of those cases where he could not even be vigorous when his argument was bad. After a while he got started again and soon found his feet, but it was not long before he again fell into the same error. He taunted us with opposing everything in the budget. He said we were opposed to the reductions in the tariff and to tire reducing of the valuation for dumping duties from $4.40 to $4.25. He said we had nothing good to say for it. He adopted these same tactics last fall when we were discussing the question of trade through
The Budget-Mr. Brown

Canadian ports. At that time he said that we were opposed to Nelson, to Churchill, to Saint John, to Halifax and to Vancouver. This was the accusation levelled at us when we ventured to say that we wanted the American ports kept open as competing routes. No one knows better than he that that is not a fair argument to use. When he voted against the budgets presented by the former government, did that mean that he was opposed to everything that they contained? He knows perfectly well that that is an entirely wrong interpretation to place upon the actions of any group. Of course there are some things in the budget of which we approve. We approve of the reductions in the tariff, in so far as -they are reductions. We certainly approve of the placing of repair parts for farm implements upon the items in 'the lower range of the tariff. Why should we not approve of that when the matter was [DOT]brought to the attention of the house by hon. members on this side?

The minister then referred to the decrease u revenue, and objected again to the criticism

of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth. Is the house surprised at the fact that there has been a decrease in the revenues received from customs tariffs? It is only what could be expected. The minister gave us to understand that the whole trouble was the decrease in the volume of goods. Undoubtedly that is a factor, but it is not the only factor. This was recognized a year ago by the Minister of Finance when making a statement in explanation of the reduction in customs revenue which had taken place up to that time. He admitted that one factor in the reduction was the policy of the government in encouraging Canadian production. That is just as true to-day as it wras a year ago; it has had the same effect upon the revenue this year as it had a year ago, but the Minister of Finance made no mention of this factor when delivering his budget this year? A year ago we pointed out that the new excise tax of three per cent would not bring in additional revenue from the customs. It wars called an excise tax but in reality it was a customs tariff. We pointed out that while the tax might bring in some revenue from those goods that were coming in free or under the lower rates, the effect upon other goods would be to place them in the non-revenue producing class. That was the inevitable effect of the tariff, and our argument has been proved valid.
The claim has been made that the tariff rates were lower under the Conservatives than under the Liberals. In answering this argument I shall include with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis). I wish hon. members on the other side would come to some agreement among themselves as to whether the tariff has been raised or lowered or as to what extent it has been changed. Speaking this afternoon, the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) referred to the tremendous increases which had been made in the tariffs. This statement was received with great applause from the other side. How can that action be reconciled with the statements of the hon. member for Souris and the Minister of Trade and Commerce? That is somewhat important in my opinion in view of the way in which elections are conducted in western Canada. We were told in the west in 1930 that we must vote for the low tariff policy. Had the people done so at that time, they would all have voted Conservative, but they did not. As usual, Mr. Barnum was right; the people like to be fooled.

speechtext: Wihat becomes of the argument that was used again and again during preceding parliaments that Canada alone among the nations was reducing tariffs? That was the argument we heard again and again. If it was true, then this other statement cannot be true.
